Example: it's 9:30am, your neighborhood cafe is already short on cups, your phone (or the bin's screen) shows that cafe lit up as a 'bring one here, +30¢' spot — so instead of the transit bin you pass, you walk the half block over, the cafe re-fills it on the spot, and your pre-auth clears. The wash logistics stay the operator's invisible plumbing; the cup is still communal infrastructure, not your possession and not a surcharge — the only new force is letting the return price float so the crowd fixes the operator's hardest logistics problem.
plain.what_changed: Fixed the fatal redistribution drift (cups glut at drop-offs, origin cafes run dry) by making the return value float so customers rebalance the fleet, and swapped the cash deposit for a friction-free card pre-auth.

plain.title: Reusables At Your Door, Both Directions
plain.description: Employers, office buildings, gyms, and transit hubs still stock and wash branded reusable cups at their own thresholds with district subsidy, so the cup is waiting where coffee trips begin — but the seed had a broken loop: you grab a cup leaving the lobby and fill it at a cafe, so how does it ever get back to that building's rack? The fix is to design the cup's whole day around the building's two thresholds, not one. Morning: grab a clean cup off the lobby rack, fill at any cafe. Evening: you walk back through that same lobby and drop it in the return bin — the cup goes home to the building that owns it, and the building's staff run the overnight wash so the rack is full again at 9am. For the commute home, the same rack restocks late-afternoon so you can grab one on the way out at 5pm too. The leftover problem — cups that wandered off because someone didn't return to their building that day — is handled by piggybacking on the district's existing nightly route: a building short on cups by morning gets topped up, a building with a surplus from visitors gets swept, so each building's rack self-levels without anyone owning the swap. Example: 9am you grab a cup off your office's lobby rack like an umbrella from the stand, fill it at the corner cafe; 6pm you pass back through your lobby and drop it in the bin; the night cleaning crew runs it through the lobby dishwasher with the rest, and tomorrow's rack is full — and if your floor's coffee crowd emptied the rack faster than returns came back, the district's overnight van quietly tops it up. Still distinct: the cups live and get cleaned at the workplaces people start and end their day from, not a cafe-side operator and not a surcharge — the new force is closing the return loop on the building's own evening threshold and letting the existing route level the residual imbalance.
plain.what_changed: Closed the seed's broken return loop by anchoring the cup's return to the same building's evening threshold (with afternoon restock and the district route leveling residual drift), so cups actually get home and washed instead of wandering off.

reverse.title: The Cup Charge That Pays You Back
reverse.description: The district still makes every cafe ring the disposable cup as its own paid line and pre-selects the reusable/in-house mug as the cheaper default — but the per-cup money no longer just disappears as a tax. Each charge drops into a district coffee wallet tied to the customer's payment card or phone number, and that balance can only be spent two ways: knocked off future drinks when you bring or borrow a reusable, or redeemed for a cheap district-issued tumbler the cafe hands over on the spot. So the cup line is felt as 'money I'm parking that I get back the second I stop using disposables,' not a penalty. To stop baristas quietly waiving it for speed and tips, the cafe's kept offset portion is paid out monthly against its POS-logged disposable count versus its drink count — under-ringing shrinks the cafe's own cut, so the register, not the barista, becomes the enforcer. Example: you buy three lattes to-go this week and watch $1.05 stack up in your wallet; on Friday the screen offers to swap that $1.05 for a $4 district tumbler, you take it, and from then on every drink you order in it is already 35 cents cheaper before the barista touches the screen.
reverse.what_changed: The surcharge money is rerouted into a customer-held wallet that funds the reusable instead of vanishing as a tax, and the cafe's offset is made contingent on POS-verified compliance so baristas can't quietly nullify it.

reverse.title: Tap-and-Forget Cup Fleet
reverse.description: Same district-owned pool of standardized durable cups, handed out filled at any cafe and returnable to any cafe or street bin — but the $5 cash hold at the register is gone, because it slowed the line and scared off tourists and the unbanked. Instead the customer taps their card or scans a code once to open a no-charge account; each cup is tagged and checked out to that account, auto-checked-in the instant it's dropped in any bin's reader, and only billed the cup's replacement cost if it isn't returned within a set window — so 99% of customers never feel money move at all, while chronic non-returners still get charged. The operator's wash route is no longer one blind nightly loop: the return bins report their fill levels live, so the van empties the overflowing transit-exit bins first and back-fills cups uphill to the cafes the data shows are running dry. And the whole program is gated on a published reuse number — if the average cup isn't getting reused past the break-even point where it beats the disposables it replaced, the district pauses expansion rather than flooding the street with under-used hardware. Example: you tap once on your first-ever cup, walk three blocks, drop it in a bin outside a different cafe that beeps green, and you're done — no hold, no refund to wait for; meanwhile a cup that's been used forty times and a bin that's 90% full both show up on the operator's morning route automatically.
reverse.what_changed: The upfront cash deposit becomes a frictionless tagged-account auto-return with a no-show backstop, plus live fill-aware rebalancing and a hard reuse-rate gate that prevents the fleet from quietly becoming worse than disposables.

reverse.title: Cups That Live at the Doorways, Not at Home
reverse.description: Reusable cups are still pre-stocked at the thresholds where commutes actually begin — but 'source' is widened past employers to ANY high-traffic doorway (transit gates, gym exits, dorm lobbies, the district parking garage, the library) so freelancers, tourists, and the jobless aren't shut out, and the racks are stocked with the very same tagged district fleet cups rather than a separate branded set. That fusion fixes the one-way drift that kills a closed building loop: a cup grabbed at your office lobby doesn't have to come back to that exact lobby — drop it at any cafe, street bin, or other doorway and it counts as returned, and the operator's existing route is what re-seeds your lobby rack overnight, so the building never runs empty and stray cups have a way home instead of becoming litter. Crucially, the building no longer runs its own dishwasher or polices its own rack — that labor is the killer that makes facilities teams let it lapse — the operator services the doorway rack on the same wash-and-restock circuit it already drives, so the building only lends the physical spot by the door. Example: you grab a clean cup off the transit-station rack like an umbrella from a stand, fill it at any cafe, and that night drop it in a bin three neighborhoods away near your apartment; the operator's van scoops it, washes it with the rest of the fleet, and re-stocks the transit rack before the morning rush — nobody at the station ever touched a sink.
reverse.what_changed: The closed building loop is fused with a district-wide return-and-restock fleet so strayed cups route home instead of being lost, the 'source' is broadened to any public doorway so non-office trips are covered, and the wash/restock labor is lifted off building staff onto a shared serviced route.

scamper.title: The Cup Charge That Pays You Back
scamper.description: The district still mandates that every disposable cup rings up as its own visible line the customer pays, with the reusable/in-house mug pre-selected as the cheaper default the POS suggests first. Two things change. First, the per-cup charge climbs through the day for the same person: your first to-go cup is cheap, your second costs more, your third more again, so the heaviest cup users feel it most instead of everyone paying a flat blip they tune out. Second, the money the district collects doesn't just vanish into an offset — each time you skip the cup, the receipt prints a running 'cups avoided this month' tally and a small credit that banks up against your future coffee, so the reusable choice visibly pays you rather than merely costing you nothing. Who does what: the district sets the climbing charge, the credit rate, and supplies the POS prompt and the on-receipt tally tied to a phone number or loyalty tap; the cafe rings the to-go cup as the escalating add-on and keeps a cut to cover lost margin; the customer watches their avoided-cup credit grow. Example: you bring your tumbler at 8am and the screen has already knocked the cup off and printed 'You've skipped 14 cups — $4.90 banked, free drink at 20.' Your coworker grabs his third to-go cup of the day and the line reads $0.65, not $0.35.
scamper.what_changed: The flat penalty becomes a per-person escalating charge that funds a visible, accumulating credit, so skipping the cup actively pays the customer instead of merely not costing them.

scamper.title: Borrow-Anywhere Cup Fleet
scamper.description: Still a shared pool of standardized durable cups any participating cafe hands out filled and any cafe or street bin takes back, run by one district operator with a single nightly wash-and-restock route. The deposit mechanics flip to kill the friction at the counter. Instead of handing over $5 cash up front, you tap once to open a tab tied to your card or phone — nothing is actually charged unless you fail to bring a cup back inside a set window (say five days), at which point the operator auto-bills you for the unreturned cup. So the felt value is still real, but the frictionless default at purchase stays frictionless: you walk out with coffee having paid only for coffee. And the return folds into a trip you already make — your next coffee run is the return: hand the old cup across the counter, the barista drops it in the wash bin and fills a fresh one, your tab clears, no separate detour to a return slot. Who does what: the operator owns inventory, runs the nightly route, and holds the open tabs; each cafe is checkout, drop-off, and the swap point on your next visit; the customer taps once and just keeps swapping cup-for-cup. Example: Monday you tap and grab a filled cup, pay $4 for the latte and nothing more. Wednesday you're back at a different cafe, hand over Monday's cup, get Wednesday's filled, tab still at zero. Skip a week and forget it entirely? $5 quietly lands on your card.
scamper.what_changed: The upfront cash deposit becomes a charge-only-if-you-don't-return tab and the return collapses into the next purchase, removing the two frictions (paying up front, making a return trip) that kept people on disposables.

scamper.title: Reusables Pre-Staged Where You Already Are
scamper.description: Employers, gyms, transit hubs, and office buildings still stock branded reusable cups at their own exits so the cup is waiting at the start of the commute, not something to remember from home — but the building's cups are no longer a closed loop it owns and must fully fund. The racks are stocked from and feed back into the same district-wide cup network, so a cup grabbed off your lobby rack can be dropped at any cafe, street bin, or other building's lobby, and a cup from anywhere can land in yours. That solves the leak problem — cups wander off and never come back in a closed building pool — because there is no 'wrong' place to return one. And the building flips from cost-center to paid participant: instead of a one-time dishwasher subsidy and then a maintenance headache, the building earns a recurring credit for every verified cup-cycle that passes through its rack, counted by the same tap/scan that tracks the fleet. Who does what: the district runs the shared inventory and the nightly cross-route that rebalances racks and bins; the building hosts the threshold rack and either washes on premises or just hands cups to the operator's route, and gets paid per cycle; the employee grabs a clean cup like an umbrella from the stand, fills it at any cafe, and drops it literally anywhere in the district. Example: you grab a cup off your office rack at 9am, fill it three blocks away, and on your way to lunch drop it in a street bin by the park — meanwhile your building's dashboard ticks up another paid cycle, and tonight's route refills your lobby from cups returned all over downtown.
scamper.what_changed: The building's cups join the district-wide return network instead of being a closed pool, killing leakage, and the building is paid per verified cup-cycle rather than subsidized once, turning maintenance into an ongoing incentive.

sixhats.title: The Cup Is on the Receipt
sixhats.description: The district sets a single mandatory per-cup charge that every cafe's POS rings as its own line item, and pre-selects the in-house or reusable mug as the default order so the to-go cup is an add-on the customer must actively choose. The charge is set high enough to be felt, not symbolic, and the cafe keeps a slice to cover lost margin while the rest funds the district's waste program, with that destination printed on the receipt so the money visibly does something. The new piece: each customer's account or loyalty tag carries a running tally of cups skipped and dollars not spent, so the reusable customer watches a reward grow instead of dodging a one-time fee. Example: you order a latte in your tumbler; the screen has already knocked the cup charge off before the barista touches it, the receipt reads 'cups avoided this month: 14 / $4.90 kept,' and the line below notes the disposable charge goes to district recycling.
sixhats.what_changed: Added a visible running tally of cups-skipped and dollars-kept so avoiding the cup becomes an accumulating reward rather than a one-time fee dodged.

sixhats.title: Borrow-Anywhere Cup Fleet
sixhats.description: A district-run operator owns a pool of standardized durable cups, hands them out filled at any participating cafe, and takes them back at any cafe counter or street return-bin, running one nightly wash-and-restock route that rebalances stock so dense return spots don't hoard cups while quiet blocks run dry. Instead of holding a real $5 deposit every single coffee, the customer taps a card once to join; borrowing and returning are then friction-free, and money is only charged if a cup isn't returned within a set window, so the felt value survives without the per-cup sting. Example: you link your card at any cafe one time, grab your filled cup, sip it three blocks away, drop it in a slot outside a totally different cafe, and nothing is charged; keep it past the deadline and the cup's value lands on your card automatically. Every cup in someone's hand carries the system's mark, so the network advertises itself.
sixhats.what_changed: Replaced the per-cup $5 deposit hold with a one-time card link that charges only on non-return, killing the transaction friction while keeping the cup's felt value.

sixhats.title: Reusables Pre-Staged Where You Already Are
sixhats.description: The district recruits and subsidizes employers, gyms, and transit hubs to install a grab-a-cup rack and a small commercial dishwasher right at the threshold people pass through, so a clean cup waits at the start of the commute; building staff run the wash cycle on premises and own the cups end to end. To stop racks emptying because cups never come back, the building's own accountability hooks do the recovery: grabbing a cup logs against the badge that opened the door, and the cleaning crew that already empties bins sweeps stray cups back to the rack at end of day, so return is the building's routine, not the customer's chore. Example: you badge out of your office at 9am, grab a clean cup off the lobby rack like an umbrella from the stand, fill it at any nearby cafe, and either drop it in the lobby bin on your way back or the evening crew collects the one left on your desk; the rack is full again by morning. The cups live and get cleaned at the workplaces people start from, never owned, never carried from home.
sixhats.what_changed: Added a building-side recovery loop — badge-linked grabs plus the existing cleaning crew's end-of-day sweep — so empty racks get refilled without relying on customers to remember to return.

v.reason: Both sets are highly developed and concrete, but Y's additions each name and kill a real program-failure the seed glossed over: register-as-enforcer (POS disposable-vs-drink ratio so under-ringing shrinks the cafe's cut) for id1, a break-even reuse gate that pauses expansion if cups aren't reused enough for id2, and removing the building's own-dishwasher labor (the killer that makes facilities teams let it lapse) plus widening "source" to any doorway for equity in id3. Y also lands a fuller SAFE/BOLD/WILD spread versus X's SAFE/BOLD/SAFE. X's single most original move — letting the fleet's return price float so the crowd does the operator's hardest rebalancing — is sharper than Y's smarter-van version, and X's id3 stays more faithful to idea 3's distinctiveness, but X leaves id1's barista-waiver gap and id3's facility-labor killer unaddressed, so Y edges it overall.

Both sets are concrete with sharp who-does-what and numeric examples, but Y more consistently diagnoses each seed's true failure mode and fixes it within the idea's own logic. Y's idea 2 is the standout in either set: it reframes the killer problem as drift (cups pile up downhill, origin cafes dry up by 10am) rather than loss, and crowdsources the operator's hardest logistics via a floating, location-based return bounty. Y also keeps idea 3 distinct while cleanly closing the return loop via the building's two thresholds, whereas X's bold version collapses idea 3 into idea 2's network and leans harder on per-person intraday tracking; Y's developments add more real substance per the goal.

Set X diagnoses each seed's specific failure mode and engineers two distinct fixes per idea: the cup-receipt gains both a cumulative monthly tally AND a published escalating-charge schedule; the fleet's standout insight names "drift, not loss" as the killer and turns customers into a paid redistribution layer (the operator's hardest logistics cost) plus a no-sting pre-auth; idea 3 closes the broken return loop via the building's two daily thresholds. Set Y develops the same ideas competently and reads more polished, but generally adds only one mechanism each (tally, one-time card link, badge-logging) and leaves the fleet's rebalancing as the operator's job rather than solving it — less added substance on the hardest problem. X wins on value-added and concreteness while staying faithful to each idea's distinct lever.

X and Y are the same three ideas (receipt-surcharge, communal cup-fleet, workplace-staged reusables), so the judgment turns entirely on whether Y's development adds real mechanism or just length. All three Y deltas are mechanism-level and attack named failure modes. Pair 1: Y adds a cumulative personal monthly tally and a published, slip-printed escalation schedule (40c-60c) — this directly converts the shruggable flat 40c into a felt, rising total, hitting the root cause "customers don't feel the cost." Pair 2 (strongest delta): Y diagnoses the true failure of return schemes — not loss but drift (cups pool downhill, origin cafes run dry by 10am) — and adds a floating return-value bounty that makes customers the redistribution layer, plus a tap-to-borrow pre-auth replacing the $5 cash hold; new force, fixes the hardest logistics problem. Pair 3: X3 has a real logical hole (how does a lobby-grabbed cup get back to that building's rack?); Y3 closes the loop via the evening threshold return, overnight building wash, and residual self-leveling on the existing district route. X is already excellent and maximally concrete (named actors, dollar figures, vivid examples), so concreteness ties at 5. But Y matches that concreteness while adding genuine robustness and behavioral force, so it scores higher on strength and far higher on value_added. None of Y's additions are hollow restatement, so this is not a length artifact — Y is the stronger set.

seed_convergence.common_fix: Reframe the per-cup fee from a one-time invisible blip into an accumulating personal number — a running 'cups avoided / dollars saved this month' tally that makes the reusable choice feel like a growing reward rather than a penalty.

Kill the $5 cash deposit-at-counter friction: replace it with a one-tap card pre-auth / no-charge account that auto-clears on return and only bills the cup's value if it is never returned within a window.

No single fix: plain and sixhats KEEP the closed building loop and close it (evening lobby-threshold return / badge accountability + cleaning-crew sweep, building owns and washes cups), while reverse and scamper DISSOLVE the building into the district-wide tagged fleet (return anywhere, operator washes on its existing route, building becomes just a host spot / paid participant) — i.e. they fix the broken-return-loop by collapsing seed 3 into seed 2's pooled-fleet mechanism.

technique_divergence.example: On seed 1 reverse adds genuine anti-waiver enforcement plain lacks (cafe's cut paid against POS-logged disposable-vs-drink count so the register, not the barista, enforces), but on seed 3 it abandons the seed's building-owned identity by folding everything into the operator's fleet — gaining nothing plain didn't, while losing seed fidelity.

Seed 1 is the same tally+escalation as plain, only re-sequenced (charge climbs through the day per person rather than across years); seed 3 reaches the same fleet-fusion as reverse — different surface framing, same core fixes.

Seed 2 is the identical tap-once / bill-only-on-non-return fix as plain, and seed 1's 'cups avoided this month' tally is plain's reframe restated — sixhats lands a subset of plain, sometimes more conservatively (keeps the closed building loop on seed 3).

why.frame_why: The techniques did not out-develop plain because each seed had a single dominant weak point (fee-invisibility for 1, deposit-friction for 2) that forced the same fix regardless of method, so the arms converged; they diverged only on seed 3, which had no forced fix — and there reverse and scamper diverged not by beating plain but by drifting to a common attractor (collapsing the building loop into seed 2's pooled fleet), i.e. divergence-by-loss-of-identity rather than divergence-by-improvement.
